facts.statement: Trepanation is the oldest documented surgical procedure in human history, dating back between 7,000 and 10,000 years ago.

evidence.quote: Trepanation dates back to 7,000–10,000 years ago, is perhaps the oldest surgical procedure for which there is archaeological evidence, and in some areas may have been quite widespread.

Keywords: Frontal lobes, institutionalization, lobotomy, mentally ill, psychosurgery, trephination TREPHINATION, SHAMANS, AND MENTAL ILLNESS Trephination (or trepanation) of the human skull is the oldest documented surgical procedure performed by man.

facts.statement: The Paracas culture, renowned for ancient cranial surgery, was situated on the Paracas Peninsula in the Ica Region on the south coast of Peru.

evidence.quote: For example, the Paracas culture Ica, situated in what is now known as Ica, located south of Lima.
The peninsula is located within the Paracas District of Pisco Province in the Ica Region, on the south coast of Peru.

facts.statement: Neolithic excavations worldwide have uncovered more than 1,500 trephined skulls, accounting for five to ten percent of all cranial remains recovered from that era.
facts.hedge: by one estimate, neolithic excavations worldwide have uncovered more than 1,500 trephined skulls, accounting for five to ten percent of all cranial remains recovered from that era.

evidence.quote: More than 1,500 trephined skulls from the Neolithic period (representing 5–10% of all cranial remains from that era) have been uncovered throughout the world – from Europe, Siberia, China and the Americas.

facts.statement: At a burial site in France dated to 6500 BCE, 40 out of 120 prehistoric skulls exhibited trepanation holes, with roughly 40 percent surviving the operation.

evidence.quote: At one burial site in France dated to 6500 BCE, 40 out of 120 prehistoric skulls found had trepanation holes.
At the time only around 40% of people survived the procedure.

facts.statement: Archaeologists identify ancient trepanation by examining the shape of the cranial hole, the cut edges, and signs of the bone healing process.

evidence.quote: Trepanning, also known as trepanation, trephination, trephining or making a burr hole (the verb trepan derives from Old French from Medieval Latin trepanum from Greek trúpanon, literally "borer, auger"), is a surgical intervention in which a hole is drilled or scraped into the human skull.
The shape of the hole, cutting edges, and the healing process that is from the procedure also helps archeologists identify a trephined skull.

facts.statement: Physical evidence suggests prehistoric trepanation served as emergency surgery following trauma to extract shattered bone fragments and clean out pooling blood.

evidence.quote: Evidence also suggests that trepanation was primitive emergency surgery after head wounds to remove shattered bits of bone from a fractured skull and clean out the blood that often pools under the skull after a blow to the head.

facts.statement: Trepanations appear to have been most commonly performed in regions where ancient populations utilized weapons capable of inflicting skull fractures.

evidence.quote: Trepanations appear to have been most common in areas where weapons that could produce skull fractures were used.

facts.statement: Ancient societies performed trepanation for spiritual motives such as releasing evil spirits, as well as to treat mental disorders, epilepsy, and cranial trauma.

evidence.quote: In some ancient societies it was believed this released the evil spirits that were to blame.

The primary theories for the practice of trepanation in ancient times include spiritual purposes and treatment for epilepsy, head wounds, mental disorders, and headaches, although the latter may be just an unfounded myth.

facts.statement: Across various areas of Peru, ancient trepanned skulls were discovered at unusually high rates, representing between 11 and 40 percent of recovered crania.
facts.hedge: by one estimate, across various areas of Peru, ancient trepanned skulls were discovered at unusually high rates, representing between 11 and 40 percent of recovered crania.

evidence.quote: The rate of skulls being found in Perú were significantly high.
Between 11 and 40% of skulls were found throughout different parts of the area.

facts.statement: Ancient Peruvian surgeons demonstrated advanced technique by avoiding the midline of the skull, which prevented lethal damage to the cerebral sagittal sinus.

evidence.quote: Instruments and techniques used in Perú seemed advanced due to the number of trephined skulls that missed the midline of the skull.
Avoiding the midline of the skull reduced damage to the cerebral sagittal sinus.

facts.statement: Advancements in Peruvian surgical technique contributed to cranial surgery survival rates climbing over time to 80 percent.
facts.hedge: by one estimate, advancements in Peruvian surgical technique contributed to cranial surgery survival rates climbing over time to 80 percent.

evidence.quote: This reflects the improvement in the survival rate increasing over time to 80%.

facts.statement: Rather than drilling or cutting, pre-Columbian Maya practitioners utilized an abrasive grinding technique that wore down the back of the cranium to thin or perforate the bone.

evidence.quote: Specimens identified from the Maya civilization region of southern Mexico, Guatemala and the Yucatán Peninsula show no evidence of the drilling or cutting techniques found in central and highland Mexico.
Instead, the pre-Columbian Maya apparently used an abrasive technique that ground away at the back of the skull, thinning the bone and sometimes perforating it, similar to the examples from Cholula.

facts.statement: In China, the oldest analyzed trepanned skull dates to around 5,000 years ago from the Fuija site in Guangrao, Shandong.

evidence.quote: Meanwhile, the oldest trepanned skull (M382) analysed by Han and Chen was radiocarbon dated to around 5,000 years ago and discovered at the Fuija site in Guangrao, Shandong.

facts.statement: Evidence of trepanation in South Asia was identified on the skull of a child from an Harappan burial at Lothal dated to 2200 BCE.

evidence.quote: A skull of a child in an Harappan burial at Lothal dated to 2200 BCE shows signs of trepanation.
